articles.title: An 88-year-old New York widow helped build a $45 million property business across 14 buildings; after saying she signed estate papers while medicated, an appeals court revived her inheritance claim against her daughter
articles.summary: Ann Giurdanella spent much of her life building a New York real estate business alongside her husband, Robert.
articles.body: Ann Giurdanella spent much of her life building a New York real estate business alongside her husband, Robert. Married for 64 years, the couple acquired, rehabilitated and operated 14 East Village buildings that became the core of a family property enterprise valued at more than $45 million, according to a 2026 decision by the New York Appellate Division, First Department. After Robert died in December 2021, Ann alleged that she was pressured into signing estate documents while medicated and later learned she had missed the deadline to claim her statutory share of his estate, reported The New York Post and Justia U.S. Law. In October 2026, the appellate court reversed a lower-court ruling that had dismissed her case as untimely. The court did not decide that Ann will ultimately receive the inheritance she seeks, but it reinstated her petition and sent the matter back to the Surrogate’s Court for a hearing. The ruling turns on whether her daughter, Christine Giurdanella-Renzi, and a former attorney can be prevented from relying on missed deadlines because of alleged concealment and conflicts of interest. Read more details about this peculiar case, as per the reports, here:A family business built over decadesRobert and Ann Giurdanella built their holdings over the course of a long marriage. Court records describe a portfolio of full or partial interests in nine rental apartment buildings, along with commercial spaces and nearby properties in the East Village. Ann handled day-to-day management while Robert managed the financial side of the business, according to the appellate decision.The family’s work extended beyond property ownership. Robert’s obituary, cited in the New York Post, described the Giurdanella family construction firm, Giurdanella Bros. Inc., as having employed more than 40 people and helped establish Bella Tile Co. to create work for family members and in-laws. The estate also included about $1 million in cash, a Florida condominium and a residence in Putnam County.Despite the scale of the estate, Ann alleged that she received only about $133,000 after Robert’s death. She sought a larger share, reported by the New York Post as $15 million, arguing that the estate plan and trust arrangements left her without meaningful control over assets she had helped create.What happened after Robert diedRobert died on December 6, 2021. About a year earlier, he had executed a pour-over will and created a revocable trust funded with his interests in the family’s real estate entities. Ann said she was not told about those arrangements. Under the trust, Christine served as both executor and successor trustee, while Ann held an income interest but could not unilaterally access principal distributions.Ann’s legal filings describe a period of severe vulnerability after Robert’s death. She was hospitalised and later entered rehabilitation, and she said she returned home in early February 2022 while taking Lorazepam, an anti-anxiety medication. A video cited in the appellate ruling allegedly shows Christine presenting estate documents to Ann, who signs them while visibly medicated and impaired, without reading or understanding their terms.Those documents included a waiver and consent to probate, as well as proposed mirror-image will and trust documents for Ann. Ann alleged that the family’s longtime attorney, Gregg Weiss, prepared the papers but never gave her drafts in advance, reviewed them with her or explained their legal consequences. Weiss has denied the allegations, calling them baseless, according to the New York Post.The missed legal deadlineUnder New York law, a surviving spouse generally must file a notice electing a share of the deceased spouse’s estate within six months after letters testamentary are issued, and no later than two years after death. The court may extend the deadline for good cause, but not beyond one year after letters are issued.Robert’s letters testamentary were issued in March 2022, naming Christine as executor. Ann did not file her notice of election until November 2024, after she retained new counsel in September 2024. By then, the statutory deadline had long passed, and the appellate court agreed that her election notice was untimely.The central question was therefore not whether Ann filed late. It was whether Christine and Weiss could still rely on that lateness if Ann could prove that their alleged failure to disclose key information prevented her from acting sooner. The appellate majority concluded that her allegations were sufficient to allow that question to be examined at a hearing.Why the appeal succeededThe court applied the doctrine of equitable estoppel. In simple terms, that doctrine can stop someone from using a deadline as a defence when their own alleged misconduct caused the other person to miss it. The court stressed that equitable estoppel does not extend statutory deadlines; it prevents a party from benefiting from a deadline that its own conduct may have induced another person to miss.Ann alleged that Christine held three powerful roles at once: executor, trustee and attorney-in-fact under a broad power of attorney. She also alleged that Weiss acted as though he represented both mother and daughter while failing to disclose the existence of Ann’s elective-share right, the true size of the estate or the terms of the trust.The court noted that Ann was 88 years old, had an eighth-grade education and lacked internet access or training. In that context, the judges said, the existence and implications of a spousal election were not self-evident. Family conflict alone, the court added, does not amount to legal notice; Ann needed actual information about the trust, the estate’s value and her rights.The dispute over money and controlThe case also involves allegations about how Ann’s income has been handled since Robert’s death. The appellate decision estimated that Ann should have received at least $2 million from income generated by a separate marital trust holding stocks and bonds worth tens of millions of dollars during the two and a half years after Robert died. Instead, it said, Christine forwarded only about $133,000.Ann has separately accused Christine of misappropriating her Social Security benefits and taking control of the Florida condominium, allegations Christine denies. The New York Post reported that Ann filed a $15 million lawsuit against Weiss in September 2025, alleging fraud, legal malpractice and negligence. Christine’s lawyers have pointed to earlier court rulings rejecting Ann’s claims, while Weiss has denied wrongdoing.The appellate ruling does not resolve those accusations. It restores Ann’s ability to pursue her inheritance claim and requires a hearing on the facts. That means the dispute will continue, with questions about disclosure, capacity, fiduciary duty and the true value of the estate likely to remain central.What the ruling meansFor Ann, the decision is not a final victory, but it is a meaningful second chance. The court found that her allegations, if proven, could support a claim that she was prevented from protecting her legal rights by people she reasonably relied on during a period of grief, illness and cognitive vulnerability.For older adults and surviving spouses, the case highlights the importance of independent legal advice before signing estate documents, waivers or powers of attorney. It also underscores that executors, trustees and attorneys owe duties of loyalty, care and full disclosure, especially when family members hold conflicting roles.The Giurdanella case began as a family disagreement over a $45 million East Village property empire. It has become a test of whether New York’s estate deadlines can be used against a widow who says she never understood what she was signing. The appeals court has now decided that a court must hear her side of that story.You use AI every day. Now get your AI Quotient. Take the AIQ test.

articles.title: Ja Rule funded a six-classroom block at a Ghanaian school after storm damage forced students into a shift system; the new building was inaugurated in 2025
articles.summary: American rapper Ja Rule has sponsored a 6-classroom block at Nuaso Anglican Basic School in Ghana, helping to fix years of disruption caused by storm
articles.body: American rapper Ja Rule has sponsored a 6-classroom block at Nuaso Anglican Basic School in Ghana, helping to fix years of disruption caused by storm damage and a shortage of teaching space. The facility was opened in April 2025 and was developed in partnership with education charity Pencils of Promise after pupils were forced to learn under a shift system. The new building offers a more stable learning environment, enabling students to be in classrooms more and giving the school the opportunity to deal with attendance problems that had hampered its educational progress.How Ja Rule's classroom block transformed education at NuasoThe new building has solved the problem that the Nuaso Anglican Basic School has had for several years. The school’s main classroom block was destroyed by a heavy downpour leaving pupils without adequate facilities thus authorities had to introduce a shift system to accommodate the children, MyJoyOnline reports.The damage had a direct effect on the amount of time students could spend learning. With classrooms insufficient to accommodate everyone simultaneously, pupils had to attend school in separate groups, reducing their instructional hours.The Ghana News Agency reported that the school had operated under the shift system for 4 years before the project was completed. The arrangement cut teaching time by half and contributed to truancy and other difficulties among pupils.The resulting shift system reduced the time available for lessons and contributed to absenteeism. School officials hoped the replacement facility would allow children to attend for full instructional hours, helping them compete academically with pupils in other schools.Ja Rule and Pencils of Promise brought the project togetherThe classroom block was developed through a partnership between Ja Rule and Pencils of Promise, an international non-profit organisation focused on improving access to education.The Ghana News Agency reported that the rapper had travelled to Nuaso with his wife, Aisha Atkins, to participate in the groundbreaking ceremony. The project was formally launched on 10 April 2024, marking the beginning of construction.At the time, Ja Rule expressed his enthusiasm for contributing to education in Ghana, describing it as an important foundation for communities. He also indicated that the classroom project was only the beginning of his involvement in educational initiatives.Pencils of Promise chief executive Kailee Scales said the organisation wanted children to have access to safe learning environments where they could develop the knowledge and skills needed to become responsible citizens.The partnership also involved contributions from the local community. According to the Ghana News Agency, Ja Rule and Pencils of Promise were expected to cover 80% of the construction costs, while the community would contribute the remaining 20% through labour, food for workers and building materials.What is offered by the completed classroom blockThe completed facility was inaugurated on 1 April 2025, when Ja Rule returned to Ghana to formally hand it over to the school. The building provided pupils with a safe and more suitable place to learn, replacing the makeshift arrangements that had followed the destruction of the original classroom block.According to the Ghana News Agency, the new facility was furnished with dual desks and learning materials. It also included an 8-unit water closet toilet facility, providing additional sanitation infrastructure for the school.Freeman Gobah, Ghana Country Director of Pencils of Promise, said the new classrooms and accompanying facilities would address infrastructure-related challenges and help reduce problems with enrolment and attendance.The building's completion was also significant for teachers, who could now organise lessons without the same restrictions imposed by inadequate classroom space.Ja Rule's plans extend beyond classroom constructionDuring the inauguration, Ja Rule indicated that his interest in supporting the Nuaso community extended beyond providing classrooms.As reported by Daily Guide Network, the rapper expressed interest in developing additional facilities connected to film, music, arts and sports. He also discussed the possibility of building a gymnasium and spaces where pupils could practise music, dance and other creative activities.The inauguration was attended by local and traditional leaders, with the rapper and his wife also paying a courtesy visit to Nene Sakite II, the Konor of Manya Krobo, before the ceremony. The community presented Ja Rule with traditional gifts in recognition of his contribution.The Ghana News Agency reported that Tettey welcomed the intervention and expressed gratitude to Ja Rule, Aisha Atkins and Pencils of Promise for supporting the school.For Pencils of Promise, the Nuaso project also formed part of a wider effort to improve educational conditions in Ghana. During Ja Rule's visit to Ghana in April 2025, the organisation highlighted its broader activities across the Eastern, Volta and Oti regions. Its country director said it had completed 206 classroom blocks across 206 communities over 13 years, with interventions reaching approximately 60,000 children.You use AI every day. articles.title: ‘Call me senator’: How Abdul El-Sayed beat Trump’s hate to create history
articles.summary: The 42-year-old Democrat has defeated Republican Mike Rogers to become the first Muslim senator in the US.
articles.body:
Abdul El-Sayed had an uncomfortable message for US President Donald Trump and Vice President JD Vance as he celebrated his historic election victory in Michigan.

They had used a range of racist labels and rhetoric to target El-Sayed ahead of the midterm elections, which he was contesting against Trump’s handpicked candidate, Mike Rogers. Trump mocked his name, and said that as president, he could call the Michigan physician and former public health official anything he wanted. Trump called El-Sayed a “jihadist”, while Vance described him as a “psychopath”.

Now, the 42-year-old winner of the Michigan race pointed out, they would soon need to address him as a senator.

“JD, habibi [Arabic term of endearment], it is an irony – you are constitutionally obligated to swear me in in January,” El-Sayed told cheering supporters in the early hours of Wednesday, shortly after he was projected to win the highly contested race.

“Donald, I know you struggle with my name, so when JD swears me in, you can call me ‘senator’. May we never have to see the likes of you in Michigan again.”

The Democrat’s victory over Republican Rogers on Tuesday made him the first Muslim elected to the US Senate, following a campaign marked by attacks on his faith and criticism of his opposition to US military adventurism in the Middle East, and Washington’s support of Israel.

“To all the parents who struggled to explain why the president openly mocks someone for their name or how they pray, let them know tomorrow that the bad guys lost,” he said in his victory speech.

Political analyst Rami Khouri says Abdul El-Sayed’s election to the US Senate could mark a historic turning point in attitudes towards Muslim and Arab Americans. Khouri, a non-resident Senior Fellow at the Arab Center Washington DC, said El-Sayed’s victory alongside New York Mayor Zohran Mamdani’s electoral success last year demonstrated the growing influence of Muslim and Arab American politicians.

“This is going to have huge implications for driving down anti-Arab, anti-Islamic sentiments,” Khouri told Al Jazeera.

But beyond the historic significance of his election, El-Sayed has focused on his promise to challenge economic inequality, healthcare and the cost of living in the country.

“Michigan, it just shouldn’t be this hard. It shouldn’t be this hard to buy a second bag of groceries or to fill your tank,” he said.

“It shouldn’t be this hard to pay your taxes and know that that money is going to be spent on you and your kids instead of dropping bombs on somebody else and their kids.”

The physician and public health official is set to win more than 52 percent of the vote with more than 95 percent of votes tallied.

His victory is seen as a breakthrough for progressives in the Democratic Party, who have increasingly challenged the party’s status quo over economic inequality and US wars abroad, including steadfast support for Israel.

Moreover, his win carries particular electoral significance, as Michigan is seen as a swing state that Trump won comfortably just two years ago.

El-Sayed was born and raised in the Detroit metropolitan area of Michigan and is of Egyptian descent.

He has often described his upbringing as that of a typical kid in a “brown” family of immigrants — he was expected to be high-achieving and successful at everything he did.

El-Sayed studied at the University of Michigan, where he was valedictorian of his 2007 graduating class. At his commencement, guest speaker and former President Bill Clinton praised the incoming senator for his speech focusing on inclusivity and equality.

“I wish every person in the world who believes that we are fated to have a clash of civilisations, and cannot reach across the religious divides, could have heard you speak today,” he said.

He went on to become a Rhodes Scholar at the University of Oxford in the United Kingdom. He also earned a medical degree from Columbia University in New York.

Before entering electoral politics, El-Sayed built his career in public health , working as an epidemiologist and eventually leading Detroit’s Health Department as its executive director.

He later became director of the Wayne County Department of Health, Human and Veteran Services.

The incoming senator is married to Indian-American psychiatrist Sarah Jukaku, with whom he has two daughters.

El-Sayed first sought elected office in 2018, when he ran for governor of Michigan on what many considered a progressive platform.

He campaigned on expanding healthcare access and challenging corporate influence but lost the Democratic primary to Gretchen Whitmer, who subsequently won the governorship.

Despite the defeat, the campaign helped establish El-Sayed as a prominent voice in Michigan politics.

El-Sayed has advocated for universal healthcare, lower living costs and a foreign policy that prioritises domestic needs over military interventions abroad.

He supports Medicare for All, a government-funded universal healthcare programme that would expand coverage to all Americans.

His campaign has made healthcare affordability a central issue, arguing that access to medical treatment should not depend on a person’s income or employment status.

El-Sayed has also focused on rising grocery and fuel prices, criticising corporate influence over the economy and arguing that working families are struggling to afford everyday necessities.

On foreign policy, El-Sayed has been a vocal critic of US military involvement in the Middle East, opposing the US-Israeli war against Iran and calling for an end to American military assistance for Israel.

El-Sayed blamed the Iran war – which he has described as “stupid” – for higher gasoline prices and inflation, accusing the Trump administration of starting an unwarranted conflict.

He has also called out Israel’s government for committing genocide in Gaza, and argued that US taxpayer money should instead be directed towards education, healthcare and childcare.

“They tried to call you hateful if you believe that Palestinian kids should get to grow up in the land of their forefathers without being murdered by our tax dollars,” he said after declaring victory. “If you believe in equal rights to peace, dignity and self-determination, that’s not hate, it’s love.”

The Michigan-based politician has also criticised Trump’s trade war with Canada, arguing that tariffs have hurt his state’s economy, which is closely connected to its neighbour in the north.

El-Sayed launched his Senate campaign in 2026, seeking to replace retiring Democratic Senator Gary Peters in Michigan, a key battleground state.

In August, El-Sayed defeated Congresswoman Haley Stevens in the Democratic primary, delivering a significant victory for progressives and a setback for the American Israel Public Affairs Committee (AIPAC), which had backed his opponent openly.

Despite initially committing to support El-Sayed in the November election, Stevens endorsed Rogers days before the vote, drawing widespread criticism.

More than $50m was spent during the primary campaign, including at least $30m by AIPAC in support of Stevens.

El-Sayed’s win had unsettled the pro-Israel establishment, Yousef Munayyer, senior fellow at Arab Center Washington DC, told Al Jazeera.

“It absolutely eviscerates the climate of intimidation that has totally clouded American politics when it comes to challenging the US-Israel relationship,” he said.

Similar to his unsuccessful run for governor, El-Sayed’s campaign focused on tackling the rising cost of living, expanding healthcare access and reducing corporate influence in Washington.

He also called for ending US military assistance to Israel, putting him at odds with sections of his own Democratic Party.

His campaign also faced Islamophobic attacks and accusations of anti-Semitism.

Following his primary victory, far-right commentators had seized on his use of the Arabic expression “inshallah”, meaning “God willing”, to portray him as a religious threat to the United States.

Trump accused El-Sayed of hating Jews and Israel, while his Republican opponent, Rogers, alleged that he had sympathies and links to the Muslim Brotherhood.

In the last televised debate in October, Rogers suggested El-Sayed had the same supporters as groups like Hamas, implying his platform was a threat to “national security”. El-Sayed vehemently denied the allegations.

On Wednesday, he hit back at those who had tried to weaponise his faith and ethnicity against him.

“We don’t want our money sent to do apartheid, or genocide, or war,” El-Sayed said. Until now, he said, his campaign had used “inshallah” to emphasise their hopes for victory. “But today, tonight, we can turn that inshallah into alhamdulillah [praise be to God].”

articles.title: The antisemitism horseshoe is playing out in real time — from New York to Paris and beyond
articles.summary: France logged roughly 1,320 antisemitic incidents in 2025 while swastika graffiti clusters and intifada calls spread across the United States and beyond.
articles.body: This past month has offered a clear picture of how antisemitism actually works. It does not arrive from one political direction. It arrives from both ends at once. In Manhattan’s Diamond District on October 21, a 26-year-old Jewish man was stabbed in the back while doing outreach. The attack is being investigated as a possible hate crime; a woman has been arrested and charged. In north London around the same time, three Jewish women — including one pushing a baby in a stroller — were assaulted in the Stamford Hill area. A suspect was detained by community security volunteers and later charged; police treated the incidents as suspected antisemitic hate crimes. These were not isolated street crimes. They fit a pattern in which visibly Jewish people are targeted while the broader political conversation treats Jewish safety as secondary or suspect. WEAPONIZING THE CHARGE OF GENOCIDE FUELS AN INCREASINGLY DANGEROUS ANTISEMITISM At the same time, online and in the streets, both extremes have continued to treat Jews as the explanation for larger problems. During France’s October student-led cost-of-living protests that turned into the country’s worst street violence in years, Palestinian flags and keffiyehs appeared regularly among the rioters. Separately, a monitoring group documented more than 1,300 posts on X blaming Jews, Israel, or the Mossad for the unrest — classic conspiracies about Jewish elites, Rothschild’s and orchestration of chaos. Far-right accounts declared that "the Jews did this to France." Far-left accounts framed the same events through the language of colonization and resistance. The two sides do not agree on economics, immigration or the future of the country. They do agree that Jews belong in the story as the problem. B’nai B’rith has a significant presence with thousands of volunteers in close to 50 countries across the globe. Our B'nai B'rith volunteers globally are not reading about these patterns after the fact. They are living them and reporting them to us in real time: heightened security concerns around synagogues and schools, Jewish students and professionals feeling the temperature shift in daily life, and the same dual narratives — conspiracy from one side, delegitimization from the other — appearing in local conversations and online spaces. What shows up in global tracking reports is what our people on the ground are already describing from their own streets and campuses. SIGN UP FOR ANTISEMITISM EXPOSED NEWSLETTER Recently reported numbers show the same split in concrete incidents. In one recent week, far-right and far-left incidents were nearly equal in number. Swastika graffiti clusters appeared in the United States and Germany. Far-left and Islamist-inspired actions — graffiti, threats and assaults linked to anti-Israel rhetoric — continued elsewhere. Calls to "globalize the intifada" circulated around the Oct. 7 anniversary in multiple countries. A network of fake AI "rabbi" accounts has been pushing classic antisemitic money tropes on social platforms. None of this requires a single coordinating hand. It requires only the willingness of people who otherwise oppose each other to land on the same target. CLICK HERE FOR MORE FOX NEWS OPINION This is the horseshoe. On one end, Jews are cast as alien outsiders who secretly run the banks, the media and the government. On the other, Jews are cast as white colonizers who do not count as oppressed and whose state should not exist. The words differ. The outcome is the same: Jews are positioned as the hand behind the curtain, then blamed for whichever crisis is underway. Other minorities are usually claimed by one side and attacked by the other. Jews are accused by both, then accused of belonging to whichever side is speaking. The numbers have been clear for some time. In France, Interior Ministry figures put antisemitic incidents at roughly 1,320 in 2025 — more than half of all recorded anti-religious offenses —despite Jews making up less than one percent of the population. In New York City, Jews have accounted for a majority of confirmed hate crimes. These are not abstract trends. They show up as a man stabbed while wrapping tefillin, women punched on a London street and a community that learns to calculate risk before walking to synagogue or sending a child to school. CLICK HERE TO DOWNLOAD THE FOX NEWS APP Americans cannot treat this as a European problem that stays elsewhere. This trend is growing here in the United States. If you only watch the far right, you will miss the assaults, the campus rhetoric and the street protests that treat Jewish institutions as legitimate targets. If you only watch the far left, you will miss the conspiracy posts, the swastikas and the older tropes that never left. The people in the middle do not get to pick an end of the horseshoe and call it safe.

articles.title: Look of the Week: Glenn Close and her six-foot impersonator demand a double take
articles.summary: Professional shapeshifter Alexis Stone’s latest prosthetic metamorphosis was for at the “All’s Fair” Season 2 premiere in New York, where he embodied Glenn Close.
articles.body: Professional shapeshifter Alexis Stone loves conjuring celebrities from beyond the grave. For Halloween, the performance and makeup artist morphed into Micheal Jackson. A few weeks earlier he embodied the late fashion designer Thierry Mugler. But the inspiration for Stone’s latest prosthetic metamorphosis wasn’t just alive — she was standing right next to him. Glenn Close is a familiar muse for Stone, who impersonated her in costume as the “101 Dalmatians” character Cruella de Vil in 2023. On Monday night, the actor was dwarfed by her uncanny counterpart at the “All’s Fair” Season 2 premiere in New York. “I think seeing a six-foot man impersonate you is quite an out-of-body experience,” Stone said in a phone call. “It was ironically Glenn who was reassuring me, rather than me reassuring Glenn.” It was the first time Stone had come face-to-face with someone he was impersonating. He called it a “visual glitch.” It really was a Glenn diagram, with clear overlaps: both were dressed in near-identical custom Matières Fécales looks inspired by the brand’s September runway — a brand Stone said had “Cruella mannerisms.” Close wore a coat dress made of Burkina Faso fabric, while Stone was dressed in the corresponding blazer and skirt. Both had the same icy-white shade of bob, not to mention their matching blush placement, lip shade and pinched smize to the camera. Unlike Close, Stone is not part of the “All’s Fair” cast. The stunt was commissioned by the show’s director Ryan Murphy, also behind other costume-driven TV series like “American Horror Story,” “The Beauty” and “American Love Story.” “If there’s anyone that was going to help facilitate this, it was Ryan Murphy,” said Stone. “He really understands the complexities of bringing these characters to life.” These kinds of headline-grabbing appearances have become Stone’s raison d’être and a key part of this business model. After making a name for himself online for his full-body transmogrifications, Stone caught the attention of the fashion community. In 2022, renegade designer Demna — another kind of stunt master with a subversive reverie for celebrity culture — discovered Stone while creative director at Balenciaga and sat him front row at his March show in Paris dressed as Robin Williams’ 1993 film character, Mrs. Doubtfire. Stone’s arrival as the pudgy matron instantly went viral. Since then, he has attended several Balenciaga shows before Demna moved to Gucci, plus runways for Jean Paul Gautlier, Diesel and Boss — though never dressed as himself. No detail is too small for Stone and his team to re-create –– from custom-made contact lenses to nail the perfect iris shade, bespoke dentures and fragrances that get him into character. At Paris Fashion Week in March, Stone upgraded from VIP guest to runway model after he walked the Matières Fécales show. The collection, titled “The One Percent,” was billed as a critique of the bourgeois class. Stone was dressed as an aesthetically conscious conservative housewife with a crisp button-down shirt, A-line skirt, peroxide blowout and fake facelift sutures. As well as designing his own makeup, Stone also created the grisly post-op prosthetics worn by the other models. The budget required for these lifelike recreations is similar to that of a traditional TV show’s costume department, reaching even as high as six-figures he told CNN in 2025. As a sign of the times, Stone’s transformations live primarily on social media — an expensive investment in virality. But even though these moments feel distinctly modern, the fact Stone’s prosthetics are real and not AI-generated already makes his work a dying art. “People’s brains are adjusting very quickly to seeing artificial visuals,” said Stone, who added that he feels an urgency to platform the physical craft. “The future of practical effects is really up in the air right now.” “I really love making the impossible possible,” he continued. “Glenn is number 22 or 23 when it comes to the (number of my) transformations. I keep a little bit of all of them in my personality.”

articles.title: In 1997, volunteers started a thrift shop in Georgia; it has since grown into a $9.5 million community initiative supporting charities, funding scholarships and helping families in need
articles.summary: What began as a small volunteer-run thrift shop in Peachtree City, Georgia, has grown into a community initiative that has generated more than $9.5
articles.body: What began as a small volunteer-run thrift shop in Peachtree City, Georgia, has grown into a community initiative that has generated more than $9.5 million for local causes since 1997. Founded by MaryAnn Cox and Joan Velsmid, Clothes Less Traveled started with a simple idea: collect unwanted belongings, sell them at affordable prices and use the money to support people who need help. Nearly three decades later, the non-profit has expanded its operations, supported more than 100 charitable organisations over its history and helped students pursue higher education through scholarships. Its work also extends to families struggling to afford everyday essentials, who can receive assistance through a voucher programme run in partnership with local organisations.How a Georgia thrift shop grew into a $9.5 million community initiativeThe idea took shape when Cox and Velsmid noticed that donated clothes were accumulating at Cox's office at Holy Trinity Catholic Church. Rather than let the items go unused, the two decided to create a place where donated goods could be resold and the proceeds directed towards community needs.They opened their first shop on Huddleston Road in Peachtree City in 1997. The store was built around a straightforward model: people donate items they no longer need, shoppers buy them at affordable prices, and the money raised supports local charitable work.Over the years, the initiative grew beyond its original premises. Clothes Less Traveled now operates a large flagship store in Peachtree City and opened a second location in Newnan, Georgia, in August 2025. Its operations also include an online store through which selected items are sold.How the thrift shop supports charities across GeorgiaClothes Less Traveled directs the money generated through its sales towards grants for non-profit organisations working in the local community. Its support has reached causes involving education, animal welfare, domestic violence prevention, conservation and assistance for vulnerable residents.The organisation's website reports that it has provided more than $9.5 million in community support since its founding. It also says that more than 100 charitable organisations have benefited from its work over the years.The grant programme allows local non-profits to seek funding for their activities and services. In 2025, the organisation announced grants worth $333,250 for 56 local groups, according to local reporting.How volunteering at the store can help students pay for collegeEducation is another important part of the initiative. Clothes Less Traveled awards scholarships to students who contribute their time to its shops, linking community service with financial support for higher education.Its scholarship programme includes opportunities for high school seniors and college students who meet specified volunteering requirements. High school seniors need at least 40 hours of volunteer service, while college students need at least 20 hours to qualify for consideration.The organisation also offers the Dick and Jan Allis Service Scholarships, which recognise students who record the highest number of volunteer hours. Its website reports that it has awarded $280,000 in scholarships since 1997.The initiative helps families access everyday essentialsThe organisation's work also reaches people who may not be able to afford even the reduced prices at a thrift shop. Through its voucher programme, partner organisations refer individuals and families who need assistance. Those referred can then select essential items from the store without having to pay for them.The programme works with community groups that support people facing financial difficulties and other challenges. This allows Clothes Less Traveled to provide practical help while making use of the donated clothing, furniture and household goods it receives.From its beginnings as a small shop run by volunteers, the initiative has developed into a broader community-support operation, turning pre-owned goods into funding for charities, education and families across the region.You use AI every day. articles.title: They couldn't read or write, now these African grandmothers are solar engineers: Trained at an Indian organisation, they are bringing electricity to 75,000 homes worldwide
articles.summary: For years, darkness shaped everyday life in several remote African villages.
articles.body: For years, darkness shaped everyday life in several remote African villages. Children struggled to study after sunset, families depended on kerosene lamps and candles, and even ordinary household activities became difficult once night fell. But some of the women who once lived through these conditions are now helping change them. Despite having little or no formal education, rural mothers and grandmothers have trained as solar engineers, learning to assemble, install and repair solar lighting systems. They are taking that knowledge back to their communities, helping households access electricity and showing that technical skills do not have to come from a classroom.The initiative is part of the Solar Mamas programme run by India's Barefoot College. According to the organisation, it has trained 1,708 rural women from 96 countries, helping bring electricity to more than 75,000 households and saving an estimated 45 million litres of kerosene. The programme focuses on women from marginalised communities, including those who are illiterate or semi-literate and have had limited opportunities for formal education.From rural villages to solar engineering classroomsInstead of relying on written textbooks and traditional academic qualifications, Barefoot College uses practical, hands-on training to teach women how solar technology works. Participants learn to assemble circuits, connect components, install solar panels, maintain batteries and repair lighting systems.The residential training at its Tilonia campus in Rajasthan traditionally lasts six months. Women return to their villages with the equipment and skills needed to establish local solar workshops and maintain household lighting systems. The training is designed to make them more than installers: they become the people their neighbours can approach when a system stops working.For many participants, travelling abroad for training is an experience in itself. A 2011 report by The Guardian followed 12 women from Sierra Leone who travelled to India to learn solar engineering. Many were either illiterate or semi-literate and had previously worked as subsistence farmers. After completing their training, they returned to assemble 1,500 household solar units.One of the women, Mary Dawo, described how surprising the idea of solar engineering had been to her. She said she wanted to be part of it. Another participant, Fatmata Koroma, recalled how darkness had once brought snakes, rodents and insects into homes, while children were unable to study comfortably after sunset.The women bringing light back homeThe transformation was particularly visible in southern Tanzania, where six women from remote villages in the Mtwara and Lindi districts trained at Barefoot College in India through the UN Women-supported Rural Women Light Up Africa initiative. After six months of training, the women returned as solar engineers and began installing solar lighting systems in their communities. UN Women's account reported that 69 households in Chekeleni village had already received solar-powered lighting, while work was continuing in two other villages, Nitekela and Mkwajuni.The systems provided households with a solar panel, a battery, a charger and three lamps. Families could pay for the equipment in instalments over five years, while a community savings arrangement helped cover the women's stipends and maintenance costs. The engineers were also expected to remain responsible for repairs and upkeep, ensuring that the systems would continue working long after installation.The change was not limited to the arrival of electric lights. Children could study after sunset, women could cook and complete household tasks more comfortably, and families felt safer in their homes. Perhaps one of the most moving details in the UN Women report came from a 10-year-old girl in Chekeleni, who spoke about watching her mother return from training as an engineer and community leader. She said that when she grew up, she wanted to become a leader too, possibly even the president.In Sierra Leone, the women trained by Barefoot College also began taking responsibility for the technology they had learnt to operate. The Guardian reported that Nancy Kanu, one of the programme's graduates, became a chief solar engineer and taught other women. She remained available to repair faults, replace bulbs and help villagers charge their phones. The work was no longer simply about bringing equipment into a village; it was about building local expertise so communities would not have to depend on outsiders for every repair.More than electricityThe programme's significance goes beyond the number of homes receiving solar power. Research published in Nature Energy in May 2024 examined the Solar Mamas programme in Zanzibar and explored how it challenged established gender roles in technical work. The researchers found that training rural women as solar technicians could help disrupt the assumption that engineering and energy-related work belong primarily to men.The study also highlighted why the programme selects women who are established residents of their villages. Their long-term presence makes it possible for communities to rely on them for maintenance and repairs. However, the research noted that entrenched patriarchal attitudes can create obstacles, with some women facing pressure to withdraw from training.For the women who complete it, the work can bring recognition and a new role within their communities. They are no longer seen only through the responsibilities traditionally assigned to them at home. They are technicians, problem-solvers and trainers whose knowledge is essential to the functioning of local infrastructure.Barefoot College's programme is now also expanding its training network in Africa, with vocational training centres planned or supported in countries including Senegal, Burkina Faso, Liberia and Tanzania. The organisation says these centres will help train more rural women and extend access to solar technology in communities that remain beyond reliable electricity networks.You use AI every day. articles.title: How a district in Florida used turned toy rabbits into Robots to control growing population of Burmese pythons and protect Everglades
articles.summary: In 2025, Florida researchers turned toy rabbits into python lures.
articles.body: ​In 2025, Florida researchers turned toy rabbits into python lures. The South Florida Water Management District and University of Florida tested robotic decoys to help locate invasive Burmese pythons in the Everglades. Fitted with motors, heaters and solar-powered electronics, the rabbits imitate the movement and warmth of real prey, drawing snakes towards camera-monitored pens where researchers can detect them and send contractors to remove them.​The project addresses a problem that has complicated Florida’s python-control efforts: finding snakes hidden in dense vegetation. Rather than relying entirely on hunters to spot camouflaged pythons, researchers hope to bring the reptiles to monitored locations. The experiment is intended to protect native wildlife, although its effectiveness has yet to be established.​How stuffed rabbits became robotic decoys for Burnese Pythons in Florida’s Everglades​University of Florida researcher Chris Dutton removed the stuffing from a toy rabbit and replaced it with electronic components. Motors make the decoy shake, turn and move at intervals, while small heaters reproduce a rabbit’s body temperature.​Solar power supports the system, and researchers can switch the devices on and off remotely. Waterproofing was one engineering challenge, as the rabbits needed to withstand wet conditions while still emitting heat. The research is led by wildlife ecology and conservation professor Robert McCleery, whose earlier work examined how pythons respond to live rabbits.​“We want to capture all of the processes that an actual rabbit would give off,” McCleery said. “But I’m an ecologist. I’m not someone who sits around making robots.”​How the rabbits helped hunters find pythons​The decoys sit inside small pens watched by cameras. When a python approaches, the monitoring system alerts researchers, allowing the water district to arrange its removal.​“Removing them is fairly simple. It's detection. We're having a really hard time finding them,” said Mike Kirkland, the district’s lead invasive animal biologist. “They're so well camouflaged in the field.”​Previous experiments used live rabbits to lure snakes, but caring for animals in remote locations was a lot of work and required a lot of manpower. Robotic substitutes could ease that load. Field-deployment of these robot rabbits started in July 2025. If movement and heat aren't enough to attract pythons, researchers even plan to add scent to these rabbits later.​Why the Everglades needs python control​Burmese pythons are not native to Florida. Introduced through the pet trade, they became established in the Everglades and prey on animals including rabbits, raccoons, and birds. Research has linked their spread to declines in several native mammal populations. Their camouflage and the wetland terrain make them hard to detect and remove.​The robot rabbits are being tested alongside existing measures, including paid python hunters and the annual Florida Python Challenge. Officials have shown optimism about the decoys, but the reports provided do not indicate how many snakes the project has helped remove.​“This part of the project is in its infancy,” Kirkland said. “We are confident, though, that this will work once we are given enough time to work out some of these details.”You use AI every day. articles.title: In 2022, Georgia police entered a rented apartment thinking it was vacant and detained two men; four years later, an appeals court revived parts of their case against the complex that employed an officer
articles.summary: A late-night incident involving an off-duty police officer working as a private security guard has led to an important legal development for tenant safety
articles.body: A late-night incident involving an off-duty police officer working as a private security guard has led to an important legal development for tenant safety rights in Georgia. The Georgia Court of Appeals has restored civil claims against apartment owner SMRE Roswell SPE LLC after an officer wrongly believed a rented apartment was empty and detained the tenants living there. The ruling in case number A26A1353, issued on 3 November 2026, partly reversed an earlier court decision. It allows property management companies to face direct legal responsibility when security workers make unlawful entries. Plaintiffs Mario Vasquez Melgar, Villeda, and Herrera can now continue seeking damages for assault, false imprisonment, and premises liability in trial court.Night raid on rented propertyThe case began with an incident in 2022 at the Roswell Creek Apartment complex. Detective Charles Craig was a police officer who also worked part-time as a security guard for the complex. He responded to reports of burglaries on the property. Believing that certain apartments were empty, Craig called for police backup and forced his way into the apartment where Melgar and his co-tenants were living. After entering the apartment, the officers confronted the residents and detained them. The tenants later filed a civil lawsuit against corporate owner SMRE Roswell SPE LLC. They accused the company of assault and battery, false imprisonment, and failing to keep the property safe. SMRE had earlier won a partial summary judgment in the trial court. This decision dismissed several of the tenants' main claims. However, the appeals court reviewed the evidence using the rule that facts must be viewed in the way most favorable to the plaintiffs.Appeals panel breaks down legal claimsIn its written decision, the Georgia Court of Appeals brought back Melgar's assault claim but upheld the dismissal of similar claims filed by Villeda and Herrera. When discussing the forced entry and whether Craig had displayed his weapon, the court stated: "In viewing the evidence in the light most favorable to the plaintiffs, Craig's testimony about whether he had his gun drawn does not demand the inference that his gun was not drawn when Melgar was removed from the apartment." The court upheld the dismissal of the battery and trespass claims for all three plaintiffs. However, it restored the premises liability claims filed by Melgar and Villeda. The judges found that property owners have a legal duty to make sure their security practices do not put people living legally in their apartments at risk. Importantly, the appeals court also refused to dismiss the false imprisonment claims. SMRE argued that Craig was working only as a sworn police officer and was not acting as an employee of the apartment complex. The court rejected this argument as a reason to dismiss the claims at this stage. It said a jury must decide whether Craig was acting as an agent of the property owner or working only in his role as a police officer.Impact on landlord liability and police security rolesLegal experts and housing advocates see the ruling as an important step toward holding corporate apartment owners responsible for the actions of off-duty officers they hire for security work. By allowing the claims involving shared legal responsibility to move forward, the court has made clear that property owners cannot automatically avoid responsibility by pointing to an officer's police authority when a security operation goes wrong. The decision also supports landlords' legal duties under Georgia's premises liability laws. Apartment owners and managers must take steps to keep their properties safe for residents. This includes setting up and managing security procedures that help prevent innocent tenants from being wrongly targeted during searches or property checks. The case will now return to Gwinnett County Superior Court. A jury will review the full sequence of events and decide whether Detective Craig was acting as an agent of SMRE when he entered the apartment. The jury will also consider whether the plaintiffs should receive financial compensation and, if so, how much.You use AI every day. Now get your AI Quotient. Take the AIQ test.

articles.title: Utah girl missing for 17 months found at home of Oregon man who faces federal charge
articles.summary: A 17-year-old girl from Utah who went missing in May 2025 was found at the home of an Oregon man who’s been charged with transporting her across state lines with the intent to engage in criminal sexual activity.
articles.body: HUNTINGTON, Ore. — A 17-year-old girl from Utah who went missing in May 2025 was found at the home of an Oregon man who’s been charged with transporting her across state lines with the intent to engage in criminal sexual activity. Authorities acting on a tip rescued the girl Sunday at a home in Huntington, Oregon, and arrested Adam Hunter Harmel, 39, in a traffic stop about 30 miles away (48 kilometers). The missing girl told another child she met online that she had run away and was being held against her will at a man’s house in Oregon. On Sunday, a parent of the other child contacted the missing Utah girl by video — and the FBI listened in. During the call, the missing girl said that she met Harmel on social media and that he had driven her from Utah to Oregon, an FBI agent said in court records. She also said Harmel threw her phone in a river; told her she couldn’t leave his home; made her sleep against a wall to prevent her from escaping from the bed they shared; often hit her; sexually assaulted her; and forced her to remove her braces with pliers so she couldn’t be identified, according to the FBI. No lawyer for Harmel was listed in court records. The federal public defender’s office in Utah declined to comment when The Associated Press asked if it represented Harmel. The AP also reached out through social media to someone believed to be related to Harmel.

articles.title: Cyberattack on French blood bank fridges thwarted before damage to products and samples
articles.summary: A cyberattack on several blood banks tried  to raise temperatures but was thwarted before it could do any damage, French authorities said.
articles.body: A cyberattack on several blood banks sought to raise temperatures to extremely high levels but was thwarted before it could do any damage to blood products or samples, French authorities said. The incident comes after supermarkets in a number of European countries reported this week that their fridges and freezers warmed up after they were remotely taken over, resulting in tons of spoiled food at a total cost of millions of dollars (euros). The French Blood Establishment, or EFS, said “temperature and defrosting thresholds were raised to extremely high levels” on Monday at three of its cold-storage sites for plasma, in a statement released late Tuesday. “No health consequences have been identified, and no blood products were lost,” it said. The cyberattack hit a supplier of refrigeration equipment at three EFS sites. The products stored were bags of plasma intended for transfusions and plasma used to manufacture medicines, and were either transferred or secured, the statement said. “Monitoring and alarm systems quickly detected the anomalies, allowing staff to take action to ensure that no blood products or samples were compromised,” it said. The EFS said blood collection and distribution operations remain uninterrupted, ensuring continued services for patients at hospitals and other healthcare. France’s national cybersecurity agency and the Health Ministry are investigating the incident.

articles.title: Hebron’s Israeli rooftop settlers threaten the city’s Palestinian identity
articles.summary: Israeli settlers have expanded in Hebron’s Old City, with Palestinian residents’ presence under threat.
articles.body:
Hebron, occupied West Bank – Yusef al-Khatib, 65, never expected that the building that housed the tailoring shop he inherited from his father, and where he has spent most of his life, would be swallowed up by an illegal Israeli settlement in Hebron’s Old City.

He continues to practice the trade that has been part of his family’s history for decades. But the settlers in newly erected prefabricated structures on the rooftops over his shop have created uncertainty about the future of his tailoring business.

Yusuf said his father began working at the business about 80 years ago, and when he was just five years old, he began helping in the shop. Nearly 60 years later, he is still working there.

“This shop is my livelihood and the livelihood of my family. It enabled me to raise my children and provide them with an education,” he told Al Jazeera.

Hebron’s Old City has had a settler presence since 1978, but these illegal outposts have extended since then to cover a wider area. About 500 settlers live in the Old City, despite it being illegal under international law, with Palestinians living there fearing that they will eventually engulf the whole of Hebron.

Over the years, Yusuf has witnessed major changes in the Old City, from the closure of markets and streets to Palestinians to the establishment of Israeli settlement outposts right in the heart of Hebron.

The Palestinian businesses located on Shalala Street, the main entrance to Hebron’s Old City, are adjacent to Shuhada Street, which has been closed to Palestinians since 1994, after an Israeli settler killed 29 Palestinians as they prayed at the city’s Ibrahimi Mosque.

Settlers, present in hundreds, are continuing to find ways to expand into the Old City area and force Palestinian residents to leave.

On October 29, settlers placed mobile structures on the rooftops of commercial buildings in the area, which are expected to accommodate 20 new settler units, which activists say will change the Palestinian character of the area.

This includes building housing on top of Yusuf’s tailoring shop. In the face of this pressure, his response is to keep his shop open, to maintain the legacy left behind by his father.

“It is an inheritance I received from my father, and I will continue to protect it and hold on to it, despite my fear of the settlers on the rooftop above the shop and the threats we may face.”

Bader al-Daour al-Tamimi, who has four children at university, has seen settlers take over the rooftop above his shop and turn it into a new outpost. He fears that one day, he will lose access to his shop and the only source of income he has to support his children in their education.

“Shop owners have come to expect that they may not be able to open their shops the following day, because of the constant threats from settlers and soldiers,” he said.

“Our presence here is not just about business; this is the home of our fathers and grandfathers, and part of our history.”

For Adel Mustafa al-Shuyukhi, 67, the shop represents another story of a longstanding connection to the Old City. He inherited it from his father and has spent about 50 years working there, becoming intimate with every inch of the neighbourhood.

“I know every corner of it, and I know the shop owners here one by one,” he told Al Jazeera.

He, too, has witnessed the changes to the Old City throughout his working life, watching the closure of markets and the raising of military gates at the entrances of neighbourhoods.

He remembers when Israeli authorities began issuing restrictions that have stopped Palestinian customers and business owners from reaching stores.

But al-Shuyukhi believes that keeping his shop open is not just a financial necessity but also essential to maintain the Palestinian identity of the Old City. He wants his children to continue running the shop when he dies, just as his father left it to him.

“Despite all the restrictions, we are standing firm and do not want to leave our shops,” he said. “I have told my children that if anything happens to me, they should come and open the shop so that it remains open and we do not abandon it.”

From the division of Hebron to expansion

Issa Amro, 46, an anti-settlement activist and founder of the Youth Against Settlements group, places the current expansion in a broader historical context dating back to the 1994 Ibrahimi Mosque massacre and the agreements that reshaped control over Hebron.

Before then, the Old City housed a bustling market, filled with vegetables, poultry, camels and carpentry. That changed after the massacre and the subsequent restrictions imposed on Palestinians by Israeli forces.

Amro says Hebron is distinct from other West Bank cities because it has a special agreement, the 1997 Hebron Protocol, which divided the city into two areas, H1 and H2.

Under the agreement, roughly 80 percent of the city came under H1, where the Palestinian Authority has civil and security responsibilities. The remaining 20 percent, known as H2, remained under Israeli security control, including the Old City and areas where settlers live.

Unlike other West Bank cities, settlers live among Palestinian neighbourhoods, while Palestinian residents also face tighter restrictions on movement and access to their homes and businesses.

The takeover of the Old Municipality building, a symbol of Palestinian sovereignty in Hebron, and the establishment of a military position on its roof coincided with the replacement of Arabic street and neighbourhood names with Hebrew ones. Israeli flags raised above settler buildings are seen as another attack on the Palestinian identity of the Old City.

“Settlers used to be confined to certain areas, but today, we are seeing expansion beyond the areas that have been closed since 1994, reaching the Old Municipality building and the rooftops of commercial properties,” Amro said.

“These restrictions aim to empty the area of its Palestinian residents and expand the settlement presence.”

articles.title: Dorset matchstick model maker appeals for museum to display armada
articles.summary: A master model maker is looking for a museum to take on his collection made of matchsticks and matchboxes.
articles.body:
A master model maker, who has spent 78 years making matchstick navy ships, is appealing for a museum to take on his collection as he prepares to retire.

Phillip Warren, from Blandford, Dorset, is hoping his matchstick armada can go on show to the public.

The 96-year-old, who stopped making the warships a few years ago, was 17 when he started the hobby in 1948.

He has made 544 model ships in total but his current collection stands at 450.

Using matchsticks and matchboxes, he has made a number of models including HMS Daring, HMS Ark Royal, HMS Belfast and HMS Sheffield.

The model maker has been exhibiting his fleet around the country since 1953.

Warren said: "A couple of years ago now, I built a model and wasn't entirely happy with it.

"The standard and particularly the painting, I was finding a bit tricky at my age.

"So I thought there's no good going making things that aren't perfect, so I stopped.

"I rather surprised myself by just being able to do that."

Warren added he now only does one show in Yeovilton, Somerset, each year "which we did last weekend but I so enjoyed showing them at exhibitions and shows".

"They're always very well received and they seem to amuse people a lot and it would be nice if we could find somewhere permanently that people could see them forever," he added.

Warren said he would like somewhere they can be on show rather than being locked away in storage: "I understand most museums have a lot more stuff tucked away in basements.

"But it seems a pity, if they're not going to be seen in shows occasionally, they'll just gradually rot away.

"It doesn't necessarily need to be a museum, there are these sort of visitor centres that have all sorts of other attractions and maybe one of those might be interested."

articles.title: Canada bars Russia from competing in world junior hockey championships, defying ruling that lifted ban
articles.summary: Mark Carney declared Russian athletes will not compete at the World Juniors in Alberta as Sweden, Finland and other nations joined a boycott.
articles.body: Canadian Prime Minister Mark Carney and Hockey Canada both said Tuesday that Russian athletes will not be allowed to compete for their country in next month's World Juniors in Alberta, despite their original ban being lifted by the Court of Arbitration for Sport (CAS) last week. The CAS ruled on Friday that Russian teams can compete in upcoming men's and women's world championships, overturning the International Ice Hockey Federation (IIHF)'s decisions to exclude them from its competitions. Next month's World Juniors is the first tournament affected by the decision, but Canadian authorities have doubled down on their stance. "So, if you're asking specifically about the World Juniors, the Russians will not be there." "Hockey Canada thanks the Government of Canada for today’s strong position that Canada intends to prevent Russian and Belarusian officials and athletes from participating under their national symbols in international sporting events taking place on Canadian soil," Hockey Canada said in a statement. "We will be meeting with our Board of Directors this week to discuss next steps given the government’s clear position." Sweden, Finland, the Czech Republic, Norway, Latvia and Denmark came out with statements signing up for a boycott of games against Russia as long as the war in Ukraine is ongoing. STRAUSS, a workwear company that is a top sponsor of the world championships next year, threatened to walk away after Finland announced Monday it was rallying other nations to refuse to play Russia. NHL AND FANATICS UNVEIL 'HOMETOWN REMIX' JERSEYS CELEBRATING LOCAL CULTURE FOR ALL 32 TEAMS "We have been a partner of the Ice Hockey World Championship for many years and value our collaboration with the IIHF. Should Russia’s national team participate in the 2027 World Championship in Germany as a result of the CAS ruling, we will forgo all logo exposure associated with the tournament. We are also considering withdrawing as a sponsor," STRAUSS said Tuesday. Russia did not compete in Olympic hockey earlier this year, the first since 2014, which had NHL players, nor was it included in the NHL's 4 Nations Face-Off. Russia's sports minister, Mikhail Degtyarev, told state television channel Vesti that "discrimination in hockey has been brought to an end," and "this place rightfully belongs to us." The IIHF said in a statement after the ban was lifted it disagreed with the decision. "We wish to express deep outrage at this decision, taken amid a full-scale war. The threats that were the reason for suspending Russian teams in 2022 have not disappeared. On the contrary, they have only intensified," Ukraine's ice hockey federation said on its website last week. articles.title: Democrat ahead in Mississippi by dozens of votes in surprisingly tight race for Senate
articles.summary: If Democrat Scott Colom wins the race, he could become the first black US senator elected in Mississippi since 1875.
articles.body:
Democrat Scott Colom and Republican incumbent Cindy Hyde-Smith are locked in a tight race for a US Senate seat in Mississippi, a state that has not elected a Democratic candidate to the upper chamber in more than 40 years.

With 96% of votes counted by Wednesday morning, Colom was leading by fewer than 50 votes, with about 50,000 ballots still to be counted.

Hyde-Smith, the first woman to represent Mississippi in the US Congress, was elected in 2018 and has been endorsed by Donald Trump. The president won the state by more than 22 points in 2024.

If Colom wins the race, he would be the first black US senator elected in Mississippi since 1875.

The race comes as Democrats won control over both chambers of Congress, scoring victories in deep red states such as South Carolina, Texas and Kansas, which had not elected Democratic senators in decades.

The Democratic Party had sent extra funding to the Mississippi race in recent weeks, seeing an unexpected opportunity to flip the seat.

Hyde-Smith led the race early on with about 30% of votes counted, but as more ballots were processed Colom started to gain a small edge over his opponent.

Mississippi does not have automatic recounts for tight races, or allow candidates to request recounts. The state also allows mail-in ballots to be counted if they are postmarked by Election Day and received within five days later, meaning the race could drag on.

On the campaign trail, Colom, a district attorney, focused his message on his Christian faith and plans to address economic concerns. He took aim at Trump's policies including the war in Iran and the rising cost of living in the US.

Trump campaigned alongside Hyde-Smith last month, saying he was there "because Cindy's doing great, but I just got to make sure. I can't take a chance".

Mississippi is a state home to the largest percentage of African Americans in the US, at nearly 40%, a group that overwhelmingly votes Democratic and reportedly showed up in large numbers this election.

Charles Taylor, director of the NAACP's Mississippi branch, told the BBC his organisation saw a huge swell in black voter participation leading into Election Day.

"We saw long lines for absentee voting," Taylor said. "We saw long lines in person yesterday. Folks everywhere were motivated across the state."

"So when the data comes back, I think it's going to tell a story that black voters turned out and turned out big."

Colom told the Washington Post in October that Democrats had not typically done well in Mississippi because large wins from Republicans in recent years led them to direct resources elsewhere.

In 2020, Democrats threw their support behind Mike Espy, a former US secretary of agriculture who they believed had captured momentum, but he lost to Hyde-Smith by a wide margin.

National Democrats are "conditioned not to care about Mississippi", Colom told the outlet. "To me, you can't be a party that cares about working people if you don't care about working rural people in Mississippi who are struggling."

articles.title: In 2021, a Texas teen died after strangers tried to pull her from a burning car; her parents turned the rescuers' courage into a scholarship foundation that has since given $67,000 to 67 recipients
articles.summary: When an 18-year-old student died after a head-on crash on a Texas highway, her parents decided to turn their grief into a lasting tribute to the strangers
articles.body: When an 18-year-old student died after a head-on crash on a Texas highway, her parents decided to turn their grief into a lasting tribute to the strangers who tried to save her life. Kenli Riney was driving along the highway when her vehicle spun off the road into a ditch and caught fire. The Argote family was travelling behind her and witnessed the crash. Mike Argote and three other people immediately ran toward the burning vehicle and pulled Riney from the wreckage. Although Argote suffered burns during the rescue, he quickly began performing CPR on Riney. When he became too tired to continue, his 14-year-old daughter, Ema Argote, took over and continued trying to save her life. After realizing that Riney had died, the Argote family gathered beside her on the roadside and prayed together. Riney's parents, Marjohn and Kevin Riney, knew very little about the people who had spent their daughter's final moments trying to save her. The family eventually learned who the rescuers were after Riney's uncle found a Facebook post describing the crash. This discovery led to an emotional meeting between the two families. They have stayed close and maintained their connection in the years since the accident.Memorial establishment honours courage in crisisAfter the tragedy, Marjohn and Kevin Riney started the Kenli Foundation in Kerrville, Texas. The couple had moved to Kerrville to support their daughter's dream of studying equine surgery at university. The foundation was created to support young people who show great courage, kindness, and leadership in their everyday lives or during difficult and dangerous situations. Marjohn Riney explained the reason behind starting the foundation in an interview with the Good News Network. "Strangers ran toward the fire," Marjohn Riney told the publication. "We exist to find more people like them." The non-profit organization provides financial support to people who have shown outstanding character, helped others during emergencies, or lived with strong faith and values similar to those Riney believed in.Growth in educational support across the nationSince it began, the foundation has grown and reached more students. According to the organization's reports, it has awarded 67 individual scholarships worth a total of $67,000 to students attending colleges, trade schools, and graduate programs. The number of scholarship applications has also grown quickly over the past five years. During its first year, the foundation received just four applications. By 2026, that number had increased to 451 applications each year, according to figures released by the organization. Along with its growing scholarship program, the foundation continues to offer special annual awards connected to the people involved in the 2021 crash. Each year, it gives a scholarship to a graduating senior at Tivy High School in Kerrville in memory of Riney.Supporting the next generation of heroesThe foundation also introduced the Argote Award Scholarship at San Saba High School. This annual scholarship was created to recognize and honour the family members who risked their safety while trying to rescue Riney after the highway crash. Ema Argote was the first student to receive this special award. After graduating from high school, she continued her education and began working toward a degree at the University of Texas at San Antonio. "Ema graduated high school this year, and of course we awarded her the scholarship," Marjohn Riney told the Hill Country Community Journal. "She's pursuing a degree at the University of Texas at San Antonio." The foundation raises money for its scholarships through community events, support from local businesses, and an annual charity golf tournament in Kerrville. Information on the foundation's official website shows that business sponsorships have helped it increase its awards from four scholarships in its first year to 22 scholarships each year. Students receiving support now come from 24 states and international regions. articles.title: In 2016, a Minnetonka collector paid $50 for a garage-sale painting; in 2025, a New York firm’s 450-page report called it a $15 million Van Gogh, and the museum maintained its earlier rejection
articles.summary: A Minnesota collector's $50 garage sale painting becomes a subject of controversy as a New York firm claims it to be a $15 million Van Gogh, but the Van Gogh Museum denies its authenticity.
articles.body: A masterpiece can lie unnoticed for decades, its true value hidden in the brushstrokes and an inscription in one corner. This exact scenario became palpable when a garage sale find was identified as a possible lost work by Vincent Van Gogh. A painting bought for $50 at a Minnesota garage sale became the subject of an interesting debate over its authorship. The work, a portrait of a fisherman titled Elimar, was later acquired by a New York art firm, the LMI Group International, which researched whether the artwork belonged to the post-impressionist painter Vincent Van Gogh. According to Smithsonian Magazine, the firm published its argument that the painting was made by Vincent Van Gogh in 1889 and posited its value at $15 million.The Van Gogh Museum’s response was blunt: it did not accept the attribution, ArtNet News reported. The firm’s case rested on Van Gogh’s working methods, the materials used and the inscription. For them, the evidence points to a series of works that the painter made during his stay at the Saint-Paul asylum in Southern France.The evidence behind LMI’s claim The painting illustrates a white-bearded fisherman repairing a fishing net near the sea. The name Elimar is inscribed in the lower-right corner. According to Smithsonian Magazine, the painting uses a thick application of paint or impasto, which MoMA notes is an Italian word for mixture. Although Van Gogh didn’t invent the technique, he elevated it to a primary visual language.The Wall Street Journal reported that Van Gogh produced an estimated 150 paintings during his time at the asylum, including Almond Blossom and Irises. He also reworked compositions of other works, a practice he called making translations. In a letter to his brother, Theo, he expounded on the creative process, describing it as “not copying pure and simple” but translating a composition into “another language, the one of colours”.LMI believe that Elimar was one such work, based on the Portrait of Niels Gaihede by Danish Painter Michael Ancher. Both paintings had a similar fisherman; this connection with Ancher is what made Art historian William Havlicek, commissioned by LMI, so convinced.The name Elimar was also connected to a character who appeared in Hans Christian Andersen’s 1848 novel, The Two Baronesses, which Van Gogh reportedly admired. LMI also commissioned a comparison between the handwriting on Elimar and the words “Emile Zola” in Van Gogh’s painting Still Life With Bible; the letter showed similarities.Jennifer Mass, president of the Scientific Analysis of Fine Art, found the canvas’ thread to match the fabric used during Van Gogh’s lifetime. The test had also identified a pigment known as the PR-50 in the sky. There was, however, a caveat: the pigment was thought to be used during 1905 or 1906, long after Van Gogh’s death in 1890. This date problem prompted the firm to consult patent lawyer Ben Appleton, who uncovered an 1883 French patent for the pigment. It had been registered by a chemical company in Saint-Denis, near Paris; this finding meant perhaps it was available during Van Gogh’s time, though a patent alone doesn’t prove it was sold.A strand of hair embedded in the paint found DNA associated with a redhead or someone with reddish-brown hair. Van Gogh was known to have ginger hair, though the test wasn't enough to confirm the person’s identity.Why did the museum reject it? The Van Gogh Museum had actually encountered the painting before LMI did when the collector submitted it for consideration in 2018, according to a January report from ArtNet News. The museum rejected the claim in 2019 on the grounds that its stylistic features didn’t carry the hallmark of Van Gogh’s oeuvre. The same year, the collector sold it to LMI.After reviewing LMI’s report, the museum didn’t budge an inch and stood by its earlier stance. A spokesperson said, as Artnet News reported, “We maintain our view that this is not an authentic painting by Vincent van Gogh. In response, LMI contested the assessment; their rebuttal, in a January 31 statement, was that the museum had spent less than one working day rejecting their 456-page report.For museums, authentication was a difficult measure, partly because definitive rulings put them in the line of legal disputes. The Van Gogh Museum had been bogged down with far more authentication requests than it could possibly examine. The Wall Street Journal reported on January 31, 2025, that requests had increased from 200 a year to around 500, and as a measure, they started accepting only 40 requests annually.You use AI every day.
